title: Choose words for the person you are talking to
intro: I can notice who is listening and choose a clear message that fits. Families and friends may use different words. More than one choice can work.
exampleTitle: Keep the need; think about the listener
example: Ari needs help opening a paint jar. The listener is named on each card. With a friend, Ari could say, “Can you help me open this?” With teacher Ms Lee, Ari could say, “Ms Lee, can you help me open this jar?” Both requests say what help is needed. The same clear words could also fit both listeners; adding a name can help get attention.
steps: Notice who is talking and listening
Start with the people in the situation. A relationship tells us how they know each other. Words such as please can be used with many people, so they do not prove who the listener is.
Tess tells her cousin, “Our cat has a new bed.”
Who is receiving Tess’s message?
Her cousin is listening. The situation tells us the relationship; we do not have to guess it from the words.
Choose a message for your purpose
A question can ask for information. A request can ask for help or an action. An opinion tells what someone thinks. Start with what you need the listener to understand.
The class cannot find the paint pots. Choices: “Where are the paint pots?” / “Please pass the paint pot.” / “I like blue paint.”
Which message asks for the missing information?

“Where are the paint pots?” asks where they are. The request asks for an action; the opinion shares a view. A request can also be phrased as a question, so consider what it is asking the listener to do.
Try the message with another listener
Keep the need the same while the listener changes. You might add a name, greeting or more detail. Do not make the message longer just to sound better. Listen to the reply.
You want to borrow a pencil. First ask a friend. Then ask a shopkeeper who does not know which pencil you mean.
What could you say each time?

For example: “Can I borrow your pencil?” and “Excuse me, could I borrow this pencil?” Accept other clear, respectful choices, including the same fitting request for both. The second listener may need more detail about which pencil.
mistakes: “Please tells me who is listening.”
It can be used with a friend, teacher or another person. Read the role clue.
“Formal words are always better.”
Choose words that are clear for this listener and setting. Home languages and dialects are not inferior.
“I must change every word.”
Keep the purpose. Sometimes the same message fits both people.
activity: Choose a pretend need: finding a hat or asking for a turn. Name two listeners. Say or show one clear message for each. Ask your partner what stayed the same and what changed.
adjust: Support: give two named role cards and model one message. Core: keep one purpose with two listeners. Extend: explain when the same words could fit both.
safety: Adult: read the words aloud when needed. Accept speech, pointing, sign, AAC or a drawing with explanation. Split the activity into short turns. A page response does not show that a child has independently performed a real conversation or read a whole book.
tricky: A child says “Please help.” Can we tell whether the listener is a parent or a teacher?
No. Either could hear those words. We need a clue about the people or setting.
Your friend says, “I like red.” You like green. Must you agree?
No. You can say, “I like green.” Different preferences can be shared respectfully.
Is “Can you open this?” only a question asking for information?
In this situation it asks someone to open something, so it functions as a request. Meaning and context matter.
faq: Must a child use may instead of can?
No. Several expressions can make a clear, respectful request. Model choices without making one formula compulsory.
What should an adult notice?
Notice whether the child identifies the listener and communicates the intended need. Do not score accent, eye contact, handwriting or one preferred speaking style.

title: Show and share what you like
intro: I can tell or show a like, a dislike or a choice. Another person may choose something different. Both of us can be heard.
example: The picture shows an apple and a pear. Ari says, “I like the apple.” Mia says, “I prefer the pear.” The words tell us each person’s choice. We can also point to a chosen picture after agreeing what the pointing means. A reason can add information, but a clear preference does not need a because sentence.
steps: Listen for whose choice it is
Name the speaker before naming the preference. Notice not: liking drawing is different from not liking drawing. We are finding the message, not deciding which activity everyone should like.
The puppet says, “I like puzzles. I do not like painting today.”
Which activity does this puppet say it likes?
Puzzles. Painting is the activity it says it does not like today. This does not tell us every other person’s choice.
Make your own choice clear
You may speak, sign, point or use AAC. Choose freely; you do not have to copy an adult. You can choose neither. If you want to, add a reason that fits your choice.
Pretend choices: drawing, building or neither. Frame: “I prefer ___.” Optional: “because ___.”
What would you choose, and how could you show it?
Any freely chosen clear preference is valid. An adult can check the intended choice: “You chose building; is that right?” A reason is optional and has no single key.
Listen to a different preference

A different choice does not make someone wrong. Repeat the other person’s message accurately, then share yours. A face or gesture alone may not tell a person’s exact private feeling; ask if you are unsure.
Ari: “I prefer apples.” Mia: “I prefer pears.”
How could Mia show that both choices were heard?
For example: “You prefer apples. I prefer pears.” Equivalent spoken, signed or AAC messages work. Neither fruit is the correct choice for everyone.
mistakes: “Everyone must like my choice.”
People can prefer different things.
“A grin proves a person’s exact feeling.”
Use the person’s message and context, and check what they mean.
“I need a long reason to have a preference.”
A clear choice is enough. A reason is an optional next step.
activity: Use the two fruit pictures, then a new pair of familiar activities. Each person freely chooses one, both or neither. Show the choice in an agreed way. Repeat a partner’s choice before sharing your own.
adjust: Support: offer two clear pictures and check the intended message. Core: exchange two preferences. Extend: add an optional reason or describe how the preferences differ.
safety: Adult: read the words aloud when needed. Accept speech, pointing, sign, AAC or a drawing with explanation. Split the activity into short turns. A page response does not show that a child has independently performed a real conversation or read a whole book.
tricky: The puppet says, “I do not like running today.” Does it say it likes running?
No. Do not changes the message. It also does not tell us every activity the puppet likes.
Mia chooses neither drawing nor building. Is that automatically incorrect?
No. Neither is a valid personal choice if Mia communicates it clearly.
A cartoon jumps and says “Again!” What might it suggest?
It may suggest that the character wants the activity repeated. The supplied words and movement support that interpretation; do not treat one real person’s movement as proof of a hidden feeling.
faq: Must a child say because?
No. Model reasons as an extension, while accepting clear preferences without a reason.
Is pointing enough?
It can be, when the available choices and the meaning of the pointing are clear. Check the child’s intended message.

title: Find messages in signs, books and screens
intro: I can notice different forms of text and find what they communicate. Texts can use words, pictures or speech.
exampleTitle: One message can take different forms
example: Look at the printed sign and the pictured screen notice. Both say that the library is closed today. An adult can also say the same message aloud. The form changes, but the main message stays the same. The pictured book cover is another form: it names an invented story, Lost Hat. A text’s form and its purpose are related ideas, but they are not the same thing.
steps: Recognise a form and its message
A sign gives a message in a place. A book can have a cover and pages. Some books tell stories; others give information. Look at the actual example before deciding its job.
Shown examples: the LIBRARY CLOSED TODAY sign and the Lost Hat story-book cover.
Which example is a sign, and what does it tell us?
The library notice is a sign. It tells readers the library is closed today. Lost Hat is the title on the story-book cover.
Notice screen and spoken texts
A screen can carry a message, just as a printed page can. Spoken words can also communicate a text. Listen to the actual words; the device alone does not tell us what the message is.
Adult says: “The library is closed today.” The screen picture carries the same notice. This is a static screen drawing, not an interactive app.
What message do both forms share?
Both tell us the library is closed today. One message is spoken and one appears on the pictured screen.
Compare forms for the same need
A short sign can remind us quickly. Numbered instructions can tell us steps in order. Explain what each form adds instead of saying one is always better.
Sign: “Wash hands.” Instructions: “1 Wet. 2 Soap. 3 Scrub. 4 Rinse. 5 Dry.” These are comparison examples, not a timed health procedure.
What do the numbered instructions add to the sign’s reminder?
They show a sequence of actions. The short sign gives a quick reminder. Both concern handwashing, but they organise the message differently.
mistakes: “Only books are texts.”
A sign, screen message or spoken announcement can communicate meaning too.
“Every book is a story.”
Books can also give information. Use the actual book’s clues.
“Form means the same as purpose.”
Form names the kind of text; purpose tells what it is trying to do.
activityTitle: Keep the message; change the form
activity: Say “Please put books here” aloud. Make a small sign that keeps the message, using words or an explained picture. Compare what stayed the same and how the form changed.
adjust: Support: use the supplied closed-library notice in two forms. Core: make one new sign from a spoken reminder. Extend: explain when a spoken reminder might be more useful.
safety: Adult: read the words aloud when needed. Accept speech, pointing, sign, AAC or a drawing with explanation. Split the activity into short turns. A page response does not show that a child has independently performed a real conversation or read a whole book.
tricky: Can a picture without written words be part of a text?
Yes. A deliberately made picture can communicate a message. Explain what this particular picture communicates.
Does a screen always show a game?
No. It may show a notice, story, information or another kind of text. Look at the content.
Is a plain pebble automatically a text?
No. Ask whether someone has made or used it to communicate a message. Its use and context matter.
faq: Can an adult read all the words?
Yes. The focus is recognising forms and meaning, rather than testing independent decoding.
What is a useful comparison?
Keep one message the same across two forms. Then name what changed and what each form helps the audience do.

title: Use clues to begin and move through a text
intro: I can find a book’s title, follow familiar English print and notice a screen control’s label. Different texts may be organised differently.
exampleTitle: Find the start, then follow the words
example: The sample book is called Busy Bees. On the shown English page, begin with Birds at the top left, read across to fly, then return to Fish on the next line. The words and arrows make the path visible. A pictured screen uses labels Home, Food and Homes. To find what wombats eat, choose Food. These are examples of conventions; other languages and screens can use different arrangements.
steps: Find a cover and title
The front cover helps identify a book. A title is the name of the text. Opening a book lets us find where its reading begins. The biggest picture is not automatically the first printed word.
The original cover shown here says Busy Bees. Its first sample page begins “Birds can fly.”
What is the title, and what is the first word on the sample page?
The title is Busy Bees. Birds is the first word on the sample page. The title and the beginning of the page have different jobs.
Follow the print in order
On this familiar English page, move left to right along the top line. Return to the left of the next line below. Follow the actual words, rather than jumping to the biggest picture.
Line 1: Birds can fly. Line 2: Fish can swim.
After reading fly, which word comes next on this page?
Fish begins the next line. Move back to the left and down. Swim is the last word in the second line.
Use a labelled screen control

A label gives a clue to where a control will lead. Read or hear the labels, choose the one that matches your need, then check what appears. A picture on a screen may be a display rather than a button.
Pictured tabs: Home | Food | Homes. Need: find food facts. Supplied result under Food: “Wombats eat plants, including grasses.”
Which tab matches the need?
Food. Its label matches food facts. In this static example the result is supplied below; it does not play audio or simulate a device. On a real page, check with an adult because controls vary.
mistakes: “Start at any word.”
Use the starting point and follow the shown English print in order.
“Every picture is a button.”
Look for a control label and use a teacher-approved page.
“Every language and screen works like this one.”
These are familiar English examples. Other arrangements exist.
activity: Use the cover and two-line sample. Point to the title, first word and last word. Trace the reading path with a finger. Then explain why Food matches the screen task.
adjust: Support: an adult reads each word while you point. Core: trace both lines and select the matching label. Extend: compare a page turn with a labelled Next control on a safe adult-selected screen.
safety: Adult: read the words aloud when needed. Accept speech, pointing, sign, AAC or a drawing with explanation. Split the activity into short turns. A page response does not show that a child has independently performed a real conversation or read a whole book.
tricky: Is the title always the first word in the story?
No. A title names the text; the story begins on its reading page.
Does a new printed line always start a new sentence?
No. A sentence can continue across a line break. This sample happens to have one sentence on each line.
Can we assume a speaker icon has played sound because it is drawn?
No. A drawing is only a representation. Actual playback must be checked on the real resource.
faq: Which reading direction is taught here?
The usual left-to-right and top-to-bottom path for this Standard Australian English example. Do not generalise it to every written language.
Must a child operate a real screen?
Use an adult-approved screen for an actual navigation observation. The supplied drawing supports discussion, but is not evidence of device operation.

title: Make a sentence that shares a whole idea
intro: I can hear whether words give a whole message, add missing meaning and check what changes when words move.
exampleTitle: A short sentence can give a whole idea
example: “The small pup” tells us which animal, but leaves us waiting for something about it. “The pup naps.” tells a whole event. “The bag is red.” tells a whole state rather than an action. A full stop cannot supply missing meaning. First make a clear message, then notice its written beginning and end.
steps: Hear the whole intended idea
Listen to all the words. In these telling sentences, ask who or what the message is about and what is said about it. Do not decide by length. A question or a command can also be a sentence.
Compare “Rain falls.” with “The very tall green tree”.
Which gives a whole telling idea on its own?
Rain falls. The longer group names a tree but does not finish what is being said about it. Length is not the test.
Build a complete message
Keep a useful beginning, then add the meaning it needs. Say the whole message aloud and ask whether a listener can understand your intended idea. There can be several good completions.
Beginning: “Our bus”. Possible endings: “stopped.” / “is yellow.”
Make two whole sentences using the beginning.
Our bus stopped. Our bus is yellow. The first tells what happened; the second tells what the bus is like. Accept another sensible complete message.
Move words and check meaning
The same words can make different messages when their order changes. Imagine or act out the stated event and check who is doing what.
A: “The cat follows the dog.” B: “The dog follows the cat.”
Who follows in A, and who follows in B?
In A the cat follows the dog. In B the dog follows the cat. Both are complete, but swapping the animals changes who follows whom. Following does not necessarily mean chasing.
mistakes: “Long means complete.”
A short sentence can give a whole idea; a long group can still be unfinished.
“A full stop fixes missing meaning.”
Add the needed message first.
“Only action messages are sentences.”
A sentence can also tell a state, ask a question or give a command.
activity: Say a whole message beginning “The little bird”. Ask a partner what it tells. Change one word or group to make a different clear message. Compare the meanings.
adjust: Support: offer “sings.” and “is quiet.” as endings. Core: make an original complete message. Extend: swap two participants and explain who now does the action.
safety: Adult: read the words aloud when needed. Accept speech, pointing, sign, AAC or a drawing with explanation. Split the activity into short turns. A page response does not show that a child has independently performed a real conversation or read a whole book.
tricky: Does “The green frog.” become complete just because it has a full stop?
As a stand-alone telling sentence here, no. It names the frog but leaves the intended message unfinished. It could be an answer in a conversation, which is a different context.
Is “Sit.” always an incomplete message because it does not name a person?
No. It can be a complete command to the listener. The examples above mainly compare telling sentences.
Are “The dog follows the cat” and “The cat follows the dog” the same event?
No. The follower changes when the participant order changes.
faq: Should an adult insist on grammar names?
No. At Foundation, model whole messages and discuss meaning with everyday language.
What if handwriting gets in the way?
Let the child say, point to, sign or arrange the sentence. An adult can scribe the intended message.

title: Hear how groups of words work together
intro: I can keep related words together, notice what they add and change a group to change the message.
exampleTitle: Keep the words that belong together
example: In “The little dog rests under the tree,” The little dog names the animal. Rests tells what it does. Under the tree tells where. We can begin with two broad parts, but that is a helpful model rather than a rule that every sentence has exactly two groups. Read the whole sentence whenever a group changes.
steps: Keep a naming group together
Some words work together to name who or what we mean. In The little dog, little describes dog and The belongs with that naming group. Do not split the message into random pieces.
Sentence: “The spotted dog carried a stick.”
Which whole group names the dog?
The spotted dog. Dog names the animal and spotted adds a description. Carried tells the action; a stick names what was carried.
Notice a word’s contribution
A word can tell what happens, what something is like or where it is. Explain its job in this sentence using everyday words. Formal word-class names are not required.
Compare “The bird rests.” with “The bird rests in a tree.”
What does in a tree add?
It tells where the bird rests. The bird and its resting stay the same. The added group makes the place clearer.
Swap a group and hear the change
Keep some words the same while replacing a meaningful group. Check that the new whole sentence makes sense, then say which part of the meaning changed.
A: “My bag is beside the door.” B: “My bag is under the table.”
What changes, and what stays the same?
The bag stays the same. The place changes from beside the door to under the table. Both whole sentences make sense.
mistakes: “I can cut a word group anywhere.”
Listen for words that belong together in meaning.
“Every sentence has exactly two groups.”
A two-part model is a starting aid. A sentence can add other meaningful groups.
“A word always has the same job.”
Read it in its whole sentence and explain what it contributes here.
activity: Arrange “The small bird” and “sang.” Say the whole message. Keep the bird group and swap in “rested in a nest.” Explain what changed. Then try your own sensible group.
adjust: Support: the adult reads each complete group. Core: explain the changed happening. Extend: keep the happening and change the naming group or place.
safety: Adult: read the words aloud when needed. Accept speech, pointing, sign, AAC or a drawing with explanation. Split the activity into short turns. A page response does not show that a child has independently performed a real conversation or read a whole book.
tricky: In “The black cat slept,” does black tell what the cat did?
No. Black describes the cat. Slept tells what happened.
Can I swap under the table for beside the door without changing the place?
No. Those groups describe different places. Read the new complete message to check the change.
Do “The little dog sleeps” and “Sleeps dog the little” give the same clear ordinary statement?
The first is a clear ordinary statement. The second mixes the words into a confusing order. Knowing the individual words is not enough.
faq: Is this a test of formal parsing?
No. Children explain how words work together through clear examples and everyday language.
Can pictures help?
Yes. Pair a naming group with a clear picture, then show or explain what the other group adds. Read the whole sentence together.

title: Find meaning in both words and pictures
intro: I can point to what the words tell, notice what a picture adds and use both clues. I can do this in a story and in an information text.
exampleTitle: The picture can add something the words do not say
example: The words say “Rae found a box.” The actual drawing shows an open box with three shells. Rae’s name and the finding event come from the words. The visible contents come from the picture. Together they give more information. The name Rae cannot be proved by looking at an unlabelled picture alone.
steps: Find a clue in the words
Listen to the exact sentence. Say what it tells before adding something from the drawing. An image can show appearance, but words may tell a name or an event that is not directly visible.
Story words: “Rae found a box.” Use the worked-example drawing.
Which clue tells us the character’s name?
The words tell us Rae. An unlabelled drawing alone would not establish that name. The words also state that Rae found the box.
Find an added picture clue
Look closely at what is actually drawn. Name a visible detail. Keep a careful guess separate from something directly shown. Use the four labelled scene panels supplied with the earlier checks too.
The worked drawing shows the box open, with shells inside. The sentence does not name the contents.
What extra detail can you get from the picture?
The box contains three shells. That visible detail is not stated in the sentence. Do not invent where the shells came from or who owns them.
Use both in an information text
An information picture can show where parts are. A label names a part, and a sentence can tell a fact we cannot see happening. Link each word to the correct visible part.
Supplied plant diagram: stem above the soil line and roots below it. Sentence: “Roots take in water.”
What does the diagram show, and what does the sentence add?
The diagram shows where the labelled roots are in this example. The sentence tells that roots take in water. A still drawing does not by itself show the water moving.
mistakes: “A picture tells the character’s name.”
Find a naming word or label; appearance alone is not enough.
“The picture only repeats the words.”
Look for a visible detail that the words leave out.
“Every guess is a visible fact.”
Point to the actual clue, and say may or might when making an interpretation.
activity: Use the actual box drawing and sentence. First cover the words and say one visible detail. Then cover the drawing and listen to the words. Reveal both and tell what each adds. Try the same routine with the plant diagram.
adjust: Support: choose between a visible shell and an invented hidden toy. Core: give one word clue and one picture clue. Extend: explain what information would disappear if either were removed.
safety: Adult: read the words aloud when needed. Accept speech, pointing, sign, AAC or a drawing with explanation. Split the activity into short turns. A page response does not show that a child has independently performed a real conversation or read a whole book.
tricky: Does the picture alone prove that Rae found the box yesterday?
No. The image does not establish the name, the finding event’s date or an unseen earlier event.
The words say “The hen watched her babies.” The supplied panel shows three chicks. What does the picture add?
It shows three chicks. The words call them the hen’s babies but do not state the number.
In the supplied Sam panel, which colour comes only from the picture?
The raincoat is yellow. The accompanying words say that Sam wore boots, without naming the coat’s colour.
faq: Can a written picture description replace the picture for an image-reading task?
No. Use the actual supplied drawing or another available page. Alt text supports access, but should not be reported as a child interpreting an image visually.
What answers should an adult accept?
Accept ideas supported by the shown image and words. Ask the child to identify the clue rather than guessing what is in the adult’s mind.

title: Learn words you can use in familiar places
intro: I can connect a word with its meaning and use it when I talk about home, an interest or a school topic.
exampleTitle: Know the meaning, then use the word
example: Fragile means easy to break or damage. In this pretend packing example, the pictured thin glass cup is fragile. “Handle it carefully” fits that meaning. Now use fragile for a different suitable object, such as a delicate paper model. Understanding is more than repeating a new word or choosing the longest word.
steps: Connect a word with a clear example
Hear the word in a sentence, connect it with the object or action, then explain the meaning simply. An adult can model the pronunciation; the task is about meaning rather than perfect speech.
Packing note: “This cup is fragile. It could break easily.” Choices: easy to break / very noisy.
Which meaning fits fragile here?
Easy to break. The next sentence gives the clue. Very noisy does not fit that explanation.
Choose words that fit the topic
A familiar topic helps us choose useful words. In a pretend shop, price tells the cost and a receipt records a purchase. Use the word to say something meaningful, rather than listing words at random.
Pretend shop: an apple costs 2 play dollars. A paper slip records the apple and the 2 play dollars paid.
Which word names the cost, and which names the record of buying?
Price names the cost. Receipt names the record of the purchase. This is pretend play, not an instruction to buy anything.
Try the word in another situation
Use a new word again with a fitting example. Explain why it belongs. A word can fit more than one topic, so consider its meaning in the whole message.
You have learnt fragile. New choices: a delicate paper model / a loud drumbeat.
Which is another suitable example, and why?
A delicate paper model can be fragile because it can be damaged easily. Loud tells us about sound, not how easily something breaks. Other justified examples are welcome.
mistakes: “A long word is always better.”
Use the word whose meaning fits.
“Repeating it shows I understand it.”
Explain it or use it in a new fitting example.
“Every family uses the same words.”
Invite different familiar words and explain their meanings without ranking families.
activity: Choose fragile, price or receipt. Hear its meaning, point to its supplied example and use it in a new familiar message. A partner checks whether the word fits. Try a word from a personal interest too.
adjust: Support: give two meanings and a clear picture. Core: explain and use one word. Extend: give a situation where it would not fit and explain why.
safety: Adult: read the words aloud when needed. Accept speech, pointing, sign, AAC or a drawing with explanation. Split the activity into short turns. A page response does not show that a child has independently performed a real conversation or read a whole book.
tricky: Can fragile describe only glass?
No. It can describe other things that are easily broken or damaged, such as a delicate model.
Does writing a new word without understanding it show its meaning?
No. Ask for a fitting example, a simple explanation or a meaningful use.
Must a family word be unfamiliar to everyone else to count?
No. Familiar words can be useful vocabulary too. Explain the meaning for your listener.
faq: Are we testing science or shopping knowledge?
No. The needed meanings and pretend context are supplied. The focus is understanding and using words.
Should children handle broken glass to learn fragile?
No. Use the pictures or safe intact materials selected by an adult. There is no need to break or touch a sharp object.

title: Notice capital letters and punctuation
intro: I can tell letters from punctuation and notice how a sentence begins and ends. Names use capital letters too.
exampleTitle: The same sentence shows two jobs for capitals
example: Look at “We met Ava.” W begins the sentence. A begins the person’s name Ava, even though the name is later in the sentence. The full stop ends this telling sentence. W and A are letters; the full stop is punctuation. They do different jobs in the written message.
steps: Tell a letter from a punctuation mark
Letters help spell words. A capital and its lower-case form are both letters. Punctuation marks help organise written meaning; a mark can be large without being a capital letter.
Cards: m / M / . / ?
Which two cards are letters?
m and M are letters. The full stop and question mark are punctuation marks, not letters used to spell a word.
Find the beginning and the name

In these examples, a capital begins the sentence and another capital begins a person’s name. A name keeps its capital wherever it appears. Do not put a capital at every new line just because it is a new line.
The writer means a calm telling sentence: “we saw ben”.
What capitals are needed?
Change we to We because it starts the sentence, and ben to Ben because it is a person’s name. The complete written example is We saw Ben.
Notice the sentence ending
A full stop can finish an ordinary telling sentence. A question mark finishes a written question. Read what the message means, then notice its ending mark.
Telling: “The dog is here.” Asking: “Where is the dog?”
Which mark finishes the question, and what does it show?
The question mark finishes Where is the dog? It shows that the written sentence is asking a question. The full stop ends the supplied calm telling sentence.
mistakes: “A large question mark is a capital.”
It is still punctuation. Capitals are letter forms.
“Only the first word can have a capital.”
Names need capitals even in the middle or end of a sentence.
“A line break ends every sentence.”
Follow the sentence and its meaning; it can continue onto another line.
activity: Sort m, M, . and ? into letters and punctuation. In “We met Ava.” point to each capital and say its job. Then repair the calm telling sentence “we saw ben”.
adjust: Support: an adult reads the whole message and offers two marks. Core: explain both capitals and add the ending. Extend: find a name later in a new sentence and explain why it still has a capital.
safety: Adult: read the words aloud when needed. Accept speech, pointing, sign, AAC or a drawing with explanation. Split the activity into short turns. A page response does not show that a child has independently performed a real conversation or read a whole book.
tricky: In “We met Ava.” is A wrong because it is not the first letter in the sentence?
No. It starts the name Ava, so it needs a capital too.
If a sentence continues on the next printed line, must its next word begin with a capital?
No. A line break alone is not a new sentence. A name may still need its own capital.
Does a full stop make any mixed-up words a clear sentence?
No. The words must first communicate the intended message. Punctuation does not add missing meaning.
faq: Must Foundation learners master every punctuation mark?
No. Start with noticing letters, capitals, names and sentence boundaries in short familiar examples. Other marks can be discussed when encountered.
Can a child explain by pointing?
Yes. An adult can read or scribe while the child points to the capital or punctuation and explains its job in an accessible way.

title: Share an idea from a story, poem or picture
intro: I can use a clue from a text and connect it with something I know. My experience can be similar or different. Another reader may have a different thoughtful response.
exampleTitle: Use a text clue and explain your connection
example: An adult can read the short, attributed selections below. Helen Milroy’s story gives us an event about helping; C. J. Dennis’s poem begins with an ant going away from home; Beatrix Potter’s words and picture introduce a rabbit family’s home. Choose one exact clue and connect it with an experience. You may use a familiar imagined example instead of sharing private information. We are responding to these particular texts, not making rules about all families or cultures.
steps: Share an idea using a text clue

After an adult reads the supplied Milroy scene note and quotation, say what you notice. Keep your response connected to the named story. A personal idea can be different from a partner’s if both use a relevant clue.
Use Reading A below: Helen Milroy (Palyku), Wombat and Mother Earth, offered by the publisher as a classroom extract.
What might you say about Wombat’s response?

For example: “I think Wombat is trying to help.” Point to the supplied offer of help as the clue. Other supported responses are possible. This is a response to Milroy’s story, not a claim about every First Nations story.
Connect an experience without judging it

Use the short poem opening in Reading B. The adult explains roam as travel or wander. Say what the character does, then connect it with a familiar experience. Similar in one way does not mean identical in every way.
Reading B: the ant decides to go away from home. Think of a short outing, or use an imagined walk with a trusted adult.
How could your example be similar and different?

For example: “Both involve leaving home. My walk is with an adult, while this poem begins with the ant deciding to roam.” Accept another fitting connection; do not require a real personal journey or assume the whole poem’s events from its opening.
Compare responses to words and a picture

Read the short home sentence and view Potter’s actual opening illustration in Reading C. Point to a visible detail, then say what it makes you think about. Pictures and words can invite different supported connections.
The illustration shows the rabbit family beside tree roots. The supplied sentence describes their home.
Could two readers make different connections to the same home clue?

Yes. One might think of living with family; another might notice that a home under tree roots differs from their own. Accept a specific clue and a relevant connection. Do not decide that one kind of home is normal or better.
mistakes: “We must all give the same personal answer.”
Different responses can be thoughtful when connected to the text.
“Different means worse.”
Name the difference respectfully, without ranking people’s lives.
“One story tells us about every culture.”
Name the creator and say in this story. Do not turn one text into a rule about a group.
activity: An adult reads one short selection from the packet. Point to or repeat one clue. Say or show a connection, using a personal or imagined example. Listen to a partner’s different connection and identify its text clue.
adjust: Support: offer two details from one reading. Core: link one detail with one experience. Extend: compare a story, poem and picture while keeping each creator and clue clear.
safety: Adult: read the words aloud when needed. Accept speech, pointing, sign, AAC or a drawing with explanation. Split the activity into short turns. A page response does not show that a child has independently performed a real conversation or read a whole book.
tricky: Can two readers disagree about which experience feels familiar?
Yes. Their experiences may differ. Check that each response uses a real clue from the selected text.
Does a rabbit home in one story tell us where all people from the author’s country live?
No. The selected text is about a fictional rabbit family. Do not generalise it to real people or a whole country.
Must a child reveal a private family experience to answer?
No. They may use a familiar imagined example, another known story or choose not to share. Keep the comparison respectful.
faq: Do the brief scene notes replace reading literature?

No. They make the discussion givens clear. Use the attributed selections and the linked lawful source, and extend with suitable books by a range of First Nations Australian, other Australian and world authors and illustrators.
What does an adult assess?
Notice a text clue, a relevant connection and respectful listening. Do not mark a personal life, feeling or preference as the one correct answer, or claim independent reading from an adult-read task.
